D018-D020_h001.question:
It all really started after the flooding at the museum last spring—about two months after, I’d say. I wasn’t there when the pipe burst, but seeing the galleries ruined, some of the paintings warped, it just… hit me harder than I expected. Since then, I keep having these dreams maybe a few times a week. In them I’m back in the gallery and the water is creeping up the walls, and I wake up with that same heavy, sick feeling I had the first time I saw the damage.

I’ve become oddly stuck and unmotivated. I used to enjoy planning tours and tinkering with my scripts, but now even answering emails or prepping for a group feels like wading through mud. I catch myself replaying it all and getting angry at management—thinking, “If they’d fixed that leak when we first flagged it, this never would’ve happened.” At the same time, I feel almost ashamed, like I failed as a steward of the collection, even though I know logically it wasn’t my fault.

Day to day, I can’t make up my mind about simple things—what to wear, what to cook—so I just stand there stuck. And if someone startles me, my heart races and my hands shake for ages before I can settle down. This has all been going on continuously for a couple of months now. It started within a few weeks of the flood, and while it’s been distressing, I don’t feel like I’m “reliving” it constantly or avoiding the museum altogether—I still go in and do my tours, just… not like I used to.
D018-D020_h001.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h002.question:
I guess this all really started about two months ago, a few weeks after that big layoff at my company. I wasn’t let go, but my whole team was cut, and I keep replaying it in my head, thinking I should’ve seen it coming or done something differently, maybe worked harder or pushed back more. I know logically it’s not all on me, but I still keep blaming myself.

Since then I’ve been on edge pretty much all the time—like this constant low‑level fear in the background. I jump at stupid things, like if a Slack notification pings too loud or someone drops a mug in the kitchen, I literally flinch. I used to go out with coworkers, and I play in an online gaming group, but lately I’ve been avoiding everyone, not answering messages, just…pulling back.

I’ve also been having these really vivid dreams about being called into surprise meetings, people getting fired around me. I wake up sweaty and tense. Even simple stuff feels hard—picking what to eat, which task to start first—I overthink everything and can’t decide. It’s been going on continuously for more than a month now, but I don’t think it’s as extreme as what you see with people who’ve been through really severe trauma.
D018-D020_h002.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h003.question:
It started after the layoffs at my paper about two months ago. I wasn’t fired, but half my team was, and the whole place felt like it was collapsing. Within a few weeks I just… shifted. I used to love the rush of a deadline, but now even when something good happens at work, I feel flat, like I can’t access any sense of joy or pride.

I get these strong physical reactions when anything reminds me of that week—walking past the conference room where they announced it, or even seeing an email from HR. My heart races, my chest tightens, I feel nauseous, like I’m back in that moment waiting to hear if I still had a job.

I can’t stop thinking it’s my editor’s fault, or upper management’s, and at the same time I feel guilty that I kept my job while friends didn’t. That guilt is kind of constant.

Day to day, I’m weirdly paralyzed by simple decisions—what to wear, what to order for lunch. I overthink everything. And if someone suddenly appears around a corner in the newsroom or moves quickly near me, I jump out of my skin. 

This has been going on steadily since the layoffs, over a month now, but it’s not like I’m having flashbacks or nightmares of some life‑threatening event.
D018-D020_h003.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h004.question:
It really started after that domestic call about three months ago—the one where the guy pulled a gun on his wife and it went bad. No one on our side was hurt, but I can’t get it out of my head. It keeps popping up when I’m driving or trying to fall asleep—like I’m back in that living room, hearing the yelling, seeing where everyone was standing. I’m not actually there again in my mind, but the scenes just replay over and over without me wanting them to.

Since then I’ve pulled back a lot. I dodge the guys at the station, make excuses to skip coffee with them. At home I’m snappy all the time. I catch myself simmering, just angry—at the department for sending us in short-staffed, at that guy’s family for “not leaving sooner,” even though I know that’s not really fair.

My wife’s noticed I can’t even pick a shirt in the morning without second‑guessing myself. Simple things like choosing dinner or which route to take to work feel weirdly hard now. And if someone taps me on the shoulder from behind, I jump like I’m being attacked.  

This has been going on steadily for a bit over two months now. It all started within weeks of that call, and it hasn’t reached the level where I’m reliving it constantly or avoiding everything tied to the job, but it’s definitely messing with my life.
D018-D020_h004.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h005.question:
It started about two months ago, a few weeks after my apartment was broken into while I was traveling for a work conference. No one was there during the break‑in and I wasn’t physically hurt, but since then I just haven’t been the same.

I keep getting these images in my head of strangers going through my stuff. They pop up out of nowhere when I’m writing copy or even scrolling on my phone, and it’s really upsetting. I feel on edge pretty much all the time—like something bad is about to happen. I jump if someone brushes past me on the subway or taps my shoulder at the office; my whole body tenses up.

Work has become really hard. I used to be able to focus on campaigns for hours, but now I reread the same brief over and over and still can’t take it in. I’ve stopped going to trivia nights and yoga, things I used to enjoy, and mostly just go straight home. I keep replaying it in my mind and blaming my landlord for not fixing the building’s front door sooner.

It’s been going on constantly for over a month now, but I’m not having nightmares or flashbacks or anything that extreme.
D018-D020_h005.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h006.question:
I guess this all really started after that car accident back in March. It wasn’t like some huge movie-type crash, but it shook me up. For the first week or two I thought it was just normal shock, but it’s been about two months now and I’m still not myself.

I get these random flashes of it in my head when I’m on the bus or trying to work on a painting—just pieces, like the sound of the impact, or the way the glass looked. Weirdly, there are gaps too; I can’t fully remember what happened right after the hit, just bits and then nothing. When those images pop up, I immediately try to push them away, distract myself with music or my phone, anything so I don’t have to think about it.

Most of the time I feel kind of empty, like I’m watching my life rather than in it. Things that usually excite me about school or my art just feel flat. I’ll suddenly snap at my roommates or my mom over nothing and then feel stupid after. And if someone taps me on the shoulder from behind, I practically jump out of my skin.

This all started pretty soon after the accident, and it hasn’t completely taken over my life or anything, but it also hasn’t just gone away like I expected. I know it’s been more than a month, but it doesn’t feel like what people describe as full-blown “trauma disorder,” just… like I never really bounced back.
D018-D020_h006.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h007.question:
It started about two months after the robbery at the branch. I was the one in charge that day. I remember the guy pointing the gun at my chest, the sound of him yelling, people crying—but there are gaps. I can’t clearly recall how it ended or exactly what I said to staff afterward, like pieces of the whole thing are missing.

Since then, memories of it just pop into my head when I’m not expecting it—at my desk, driving home—and it feels like I’m right back there. I’ve been going out of my way not to drive past the branch where it happened, and I avoid talking about that day with my team or my wife. I even switched my lunch spot so I don’t run into certain customers who were there.

At home, I feel oddly shut off. I care about my wife and kids, but it’s like there’s a wall; I go through the motions without really feeling close. I’ve also been snapping at people—staff, my wife—for minor things, yelling in a way that’s not like me. And if someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin. This has all been going on steadily for a couple of months now, since shortly after the robbery.
D018-D020_h007.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h008.question:
It all started about two months ago, right after they laid off half my line at the plant. They kept me, but they doubled the quota on nights. It wasn’t some war or car crash or anything, but ever since that happened I feel like my whole system’s stuck on high alert.

I keep getting these flashes in my head when I’m trying to work or trying to sleep—like replaying that week over and over: the meeting, people crying, the supervisor yelling about numbers. They just pop in, and I can’t shut them off. Because of that, I’ve been doing everything I can to avoid anything that reminds me of it—no talking to the old crew, I take a different entrance so I don’t pass the conference room where they told us, I even stopped going out for drinks with coworkers.

The weird part is, big chunks of that week are just… blank. I know I was there, but I can’t really piece it together. And I feel kind of hollow toward people—my sister, guys I’ve dated; it’s like I can’t feel close to anyone.

I’m jumpy as hell now. A pallet drops or a machine clangs and I flinch like I’ve been shocked. I’ve snapped a couple times too—slammed a crate so hard it cracked, shoved a coworker who startled me from behind. This has been going on steadily for more than a month now, but from what I’ve read, I don’t think I have all the stuff they describe for that full-blown trauma disorder.
D018-D020_h008.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h009.question:
It really started about two months after my ex-husband was arrested for domestic violence. The whole legal process dragged on for a few months, and during that time the symptoms just kind of crept in. It’s been over three months now, and they’re still there, even though the court stuff is basically over.

Sometimes at home I’ll suddenly feel like I’m back in the kitchen that night—he’s yelling, coming toward me—and for a few seconds I’m not fully in the present. It’s not constant, but when it happens it’s very vivid and disorienting. I remember parts of that night too clearly, like what I was wearing and the sound of a glass breaking, but there are gaps around what he actually said and the sequence of things. I just can’t pull those pieces up.

I avoid anything that reminds me of him—certain streets, mutual friends, even restaurants we used to go to. At work as a dietitian, I function, but even when a client does really well or my boss praises me, I feel flat, like I can’t access any real happiness. I’ve also become snappy; I’ll lash out at coworkers or my sister over small things, raising my voice before I even realize it. And if someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly, I jump hard, heart racing, like my whole body overreacts to being touched.  

The symptoms have been ongoing for several months now, but from what I understand they don’t seem to match the full picture of what people describe as that more severe, long-term trauma condition.
D018-D020_h009.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h010.question:
It really started about two months ago, within a few weeks after that bad night in the OR. We lost a patient on the table during an emergency trauma case. I honestly can’t remember big chunks of what actually happened during the code itself—just bits and pieces, like flashes—but not the sequence, not the details people keep asking me about.

Since then, whenever I walk past that OR or hear a similar monitor alarm, my chest tightens and I feel this wave of dread. I’ve been volunteering to switch cases or stay in clinic just to avoid that room and the senior who was attending that night. I skip certain trauma call shifts if I can trade them away.

I’m on edge all the time now. Little things set me off—I snap at nurses, co-residents, even family on the phone. Any sudden noise—a dropped instrument, a door slamming—makes me jump like I’ve been shocked.

What bothers me is that even when I do something objectively good, like nailing a complex laparoscopic case and getting praised, I feel nothing. No pride, no satisfaction. It’s been more than a month of this, but from what I’ve read and discussed with colleagues, I don’t think what I’m experiencing fits the full picture of what they call classic long-term trauma syndromes.
D018-D020_h010.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h011.question:
It started about two months ago, a few weeks after I got put on academic probation and my long-term lab placement fell through. I know that’s not like a “major disaster,” but it felt like my whole future just collapsed. Since then, any email from the department or walking past that lab building makes my chest tighten and my mind just spirals. I’ll replay the whole thing in my head and feel this wave of panic and shame, so I try really hard not to think about it at all. I avoid talking about school with my friends and even skip certain hallways on campus so I don’t have to be reminded.

I’ve started telling myself I’m basically broken, that I’m a failure who doesn’t belong in grad school at all. At the same time, I keep going over how my advisor and the program handled it and get stuck on how unfair it was, like they ruined my chances.

When something brings it up—like someone asking how my research is going—I snap. I’ve yelled at my roommate and my mom on the phone, swearing and blaming them for not supporting me more. This has been going on continuously, but I haven’t had nightmares or flashbacks or anything like that.
D018-D020_h011.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h012.question:
About two months ago I was working on a freight elevator that dropped a few floors when a safety failed. I was inside the car. It stopped before it hit bottom, but it was violent and I thought I was going to die. Since then I’ve been…off.

Any time I hear a loud metallic bang or feel a sudden jolt, my chest just tightens and my mind flashes back to that drop. I get really worked up for a while afterward, even if I know I’m not in danger. I’ve been coming up with excuses to avoid certain buildings at work, especially older ones with sketchy elevators, and I steer clear of talking about that day with coworkers.

I’ve started thinking people in management don’t really care if we’re safe, like they’re all cutting corners, and I catch myself blaming my supervisor for putting me on that job at all. I’m more on edge with everyone—snapping at my brother over nothing, getting irritated in traffic way faster than I used to.

This all started within a few weeks of the incident. It’s been going on for over a month now, but I don’t have nightmares, I’m sleeping okay, and I’m not constantly reliving it—just reacting hard when something sets me off.
D018-D020_h012.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h013.question:
It really started after the company downsized my crew about two months ago. Overnight I went from a normal workload to doing the jobs of three guys, worrying every day I’ll be next. Since then I’ve been having these lousy, vivid dreams a few nights a week about work—alarms going off, pipes bursting, my boss yelling that I’ve ruined everything. I wake up sweaty and on edge.

During the day I try not to think about it. I avoid looking at emails from management, and I put off any paperwork that reminds me of the cutbacks. If my wife asks how things are going, I shut down or change the subject because I don’t want to get into it.

I’ve started thinking I’m just a screw‑up, like I’m broken somehow and not worth much if I can’t keep everything running perfectly. At the same time, I catch myself stewing about how the higher‑ups did this to us, blaming them for wrecking a good team.

I’ve been more short‑fused, snapping at my wife and guys at work over small things, raising my voice in ways I never used to. This has all been going on steadily for over a month now, but it hasn’t been some life‑or‑death event—just this work mess dragging on.
D018-D020_h013.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h014.question:
It started after the divorce, about two months ago, when the court finally settled everything. Within a few weeks I noticed I was different. Whenever I drive past the courthouse or the street where my ex used to work, my heart starts pounding, my palms sweat, sometimes I feel short of breath, like I have to grip the steering wheel tighter just to stay in control. I do everything I can to avoid thinking about the whole mess—if a passenger brings up breakups or lawyers, I change the subject or turn up the radio, because if I let my mind go there, I feel this rush of anger and shame.

I’ve become really suspicious of people. I catch myself thinking no one is really on my side, that everyone’s just out to use you and leave. I put a lot of the blame for how my life turned out on my ex and her family; I replay arguments in my head and get worked up all over again. I’ve been snapping at passengers and shouting over small things, cursing at other drivers more than I used to. This has been going on steadily for over a month now, and while it hasn’t totally taken over my life, it’s definitely not how I used to be.
D018-D020_h014.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h015.question:
It started about two months after the car accident in March. I wasn’t badly hurt, but ever since, I keep getting these moments where I’m suddenly back there. It’s like I’m seeing the headlights coming at me again, even though I know I’m in my office or at home. It doesn’t last long, but it’s really jarring.

I’ve been going out of my way to avoid anything to do with that intersection—will drive 20 extra minutes just not to pass it. I’ve turned down invites from coworkers if it means going near that area, and I change the subject if anyone brings up car accidents or the weather that night.

I catch myself thinking the world is just unsafe now, like something horrible can happen at any moment, and sometimes I feel like if I’d left work five minutes earlier or later, it wouldn’t have happened. I know logically it’s not really my fault, but I still replay it that way.

I’ve had a couple of episodes where I completely lost my temper—slammed a drawer so hard it broke, shoved my brother when he joked about my driving. This has all been going on for a couple of months now, more than a month after the crash, but I was told it doesn’t fully fit that big trauma diagnosis.
D018-D020_h015.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h016.question:
About four months ago, the store next to my appraisal office was robbed at gunpoint while I was working late. I heard the shouting and saw the guy run past our glass front with the gun in his hand. Nobody in my shop was hurt and I never actually had a gun pointed at me, but it shook me up.

Since then, I keep having these dreams maybe a couple of times a week where I’m back at my workbench, and suddenly there’s someone outside with a gun. I’ll wake up with my heart racing, but it’s not every night and I don’t wake up screaming or anything like that.

I’ve started going out of my way to avoid that whole block after dark, and I’ll make excuses not to meet friends anywhere near that area. I catch myself constantly checking who’s around me when I walk home or ride the subway, like I’m scanning for anyone who looks “off.”

I find myself stewing about it, blaming the building management and even my boss for not having better security, even though I know, rationally, they couldn’t have predicted it. These things started within a few weeks of the robbery, and they’ve been lingering, but they haven’t completely taken over my life, and I don’t think I have “all the symptoms” people talk about after major trauma.
D018-D020_h016.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h017.question:
It started about two months ago, a few weeks after the layoff announcement in my department. My position ended up being safe, but several close colleagues lost their jobs, and I was on that chopping block list for a while. Since then, I haven’t felt like myself.

When I walk past the dean’s office or the HR suite, my chest tightens and I sometimes have to turn around and take a different route. I keep replaying things I said in meetings, thinking if I’d argued differently maybe people wouldn’t have been let go. I know rationally that’s not all on me, but I still feel like I failed them somehow.

On campus, I routinely scan exits in lecture halls and keep an eye on who walks in late. It’s not like I’m having flashbacks or nightmares, but I’m on edge in those settings. This all started within three months of the whole downsizing mess, and it’s been going on steadily for over a month now, though it has eased a little as the dust has settled.
D018-D020_h017.options:

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h018.question:
It really started after that big pileup on the freeway about two months ago. I was on nights in the ER, and it was just…chaotic. I keep thinking if I’d moved faster, or chosen different orders, maybe one of the younger patients wouldn’t have died. I replay it constantly and beat myself up, like I failed her.

It’s not like I’m having nightmares every night or reliving it in my head like a movie, but certain things set me off. The sound of sirens, the smell of blood, even driving past that exit makes my chest tighten and I feel on edge for a while. Because of that, I’ve been switching shifts to avoid trauma-heavy nights and steering clear of coworkers who were on that shift. I’ll change the subject if anyone brings it up.

At work and even in regular places like parking garages or crowded waiting rooms, I’m much more on guard than before—scanning people, exits, looking for what could go wrong. It’s been going on steadily since that shift, and it’s not getting worse, but it’s also not really taking over my whole life or anything.
D018-D020_h018.options:

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h019.question:
It started about two months ago, a few weeks after one of my matchmaking clients was assaulted on a first date I had arranged. I can’t shake it. I keep thinking, “If I’d vetted him better, this wouldn’t have happened.” I go over every email, every red flag I might have missed, and I end up just blaming myself.

I avoid certain restaurants and bars where I used to send people, and I make excuses not to attend in-person events or mixers because just being there makes me think of what happened. I even avoid talking about that whole situation with colleagues or my husband.

I’m constantly on edge now—when I’m setting people up I’m obsessively checking for danger, scrolling through their social media, Googling them, scanning venues like I’m security. It all kicked in within a couple of months of the incident, and it’s been going on steadily, but I don’t think I’m having flashbacks or anything that extreme.
D018-D020_h019.options:

    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h020.question:
It started after the break‑in at my studio about two months ago. Nobody hurt me, but they smashed the place up and stole pieces I’d been working on for months. Since then, I haven’t been myself.

Whenever I walk past the building or even hear metal clinking, I get this rush of panic in my chest, like I’m right back there opening the door and seeing the mess. I keep going over it in my head, blaming myself—if I’d installed better locks, if I hadn’t stayed so late that week and posted about it online, maybe they wouldn’t have targeted me. I know it’s not logical, but I can’t shake it.

I’m constantly on edge now, scanning every hallway, checking the locks three, four times. It’s been going on for more than a month, and it all started within weeks of the break‑in, but I don’t have nightmares or flashbacks or anything like that. It just feels like I never really bounced back.
D018-D020_h020.options:

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h021.question:
It started about two months ago, pretty soon after that shooting at the warehouse. I keep seeing it in my head, like a clip on repeat. I’ll be driving or trying to do paperwork at the station and suddenly I’m right back there—smell, sounds, the guy’s face—whether I want to think about it or not. It’s not like full-blown flashbacks, I know where I am, but it just barges in and I can’t shut it off.

Since then I’ve been on edge all the time. My temper is paper-thin—my partner makes a small joke and I snap, my kids are loud for a second and I bark at them. It’s like my nerves are raw.

What’s bothering me most is how I feel with my family. My wife hugs me, the kids want to play, and I go through the motions, but it’s like there’s a wall. I remember loving that, but right now I feel…blank. And underneath that, I’m just ashamed—ashamed I didn’t handle the call better, ashamed I’m not “over it” by now.

The incident was a one-time thing, it’s over, but this hasn’t settled down; it’s been getting in the way at home and at work.
D018-D020_h021.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h022.question:

D018-D020_h023.question:

D018-D020_h023.options:

It started about two months after everything happened with the gallery fire. I’d been working late restoring a series of paintings when the wiring shorted out. I wasn’t physically hurt, but watching the studio burn and thinking my colleagues might still be inside really shook me.

Since then, any smell of smoke, even from my husband cooking, or seeing flickering light—like a candle or a reflection on varnish—sets me on edge. My chest tightens, my heart races, and I can’t focus on the canvas in front of me. It feels way out of proportion to what’s actually happening.

I’m on edge most of the time now—like I’m waiting for something bad to happen. Even on quiet days at the workshop, I feel tense and jumpy. I used to really love my work and small things, like finishing a difficult restoration or going out with my husband, made me genuinely happy. Lately, even when something goes well, I just feel flat, like I’m watching myself from the outside.

I also snap so easily. Tiny things—a misplaced brush, my husband asking a simple question—can set me off into sudden yelling that surprises even me. The stress from the fire has mostly settled—insurance is sorted, the studio’s reopened—but these reactions are still sticking around, even though I don’t have all the nightmares and constant reliving you’d expect after something truly horrific.

It started after that big car accident in March, when a truck sideswiped us on the highway. Nobody died, but it really shook me up. Within a few weeks, I noticed I was reacting way more strongly than felt “normal.” Every time I hear screeching brakes, or even see a similar truck on the road, my chest tightens and my mind just replays the moment of impact. I can’t shake the feeling for hours afterward.

Since then—so, about four months now—I feel like there’s this constant anger simmering under the surface. I snap at my students over tiny things, like someone tapping a pencil, and then later I’m shocked at how harsh I sounded. At home, my husband will do something minor, like forget to rinse a cup, and I’ll suddenly blow up, yelling before I even realize I’m angry.

What bothers me is that even when something goes well—my class scores high on a test, or my principal praises me—I feel flat, like I just can’t feel proud or satisfied anymore. I’m upset and on edge a lot, but from what I’ve read and what friends say, it doesn’t seem as extreme or all‑consuming as what people describe with full‑blown trauma disorders.
